  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }

  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {

Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra 
<br class="ltx_break">Predict Model Quality
</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">A solid understanding of the predictive success of
deep neural networks (DNNs) remains elusive.
For example, while many data-dependent metrics exist that seek to predict model quality of DNNs, these metrics may be expensive to compute for large datasets and/or may be impossible to compute when training datasets are not released.
A practical and effective predictor of model quality involves analyzing DNN weight matrices, as prior work has established that heavy-tailed spectral distributions in trained weight matrices can be strongly predictive of model quality.
However, such metrics lack a rigorous statistical justification.
In this work, we aim to understand why these metrics perform well, from a statistical perspective.
To do so, we employ a probabilistic framework to derive the marginal likelihood for a DNN, evaluated using only the final layer weights.
Across large-scale convolutional DNNs and LLMs, we find that this marginal likelihood predicts model quality.
To understand the role heavy-tailed spectra play in
predictive performance,
we derive the limiting log-marginal likelihood for spectra that follow the (heavy-tailed) High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur (HTMP) distribution.
We show that this limiting quantity is convex in a <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">heaviness</span> parameter, and we derive an optimal <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">heaviness</span> that empirically predicts over-fitting for large-scale DNNs.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since the introduction of AlexNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky et al., 2012</a>)</cite>, an understanding of the mechanisms behind
the predictive success of deep neural networks (DNNs) has lagged behind empirical advancements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
For example, generalization is one way to try to quantify this; in contrast to classical statistical learning theory (SLT), however, large heavily over-parameterized DNNs generalize well after training to near zero-loss.
This phenomenon extends the classical U-shaped bias-variance curve to the well-known <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">double-descent</span> curve <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belkin et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
The recent success of large language models (LLMs) further complicates the picture: foundation models are often <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">under-parameterized</span>, and do not attain zero-loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Instead, the performance of LLMs seems to be (empirically) well-governed by neural scaling laws <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, the theoretical underpinnings of which are not well understood <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boopathy and Fiete, 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Tools for attempting to estimate model quality of DNNs are extensive.
Classical statistical techniques using complexity measures such as the Rademacher complexity, Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension, and uniform stability have been largely unsuccessful <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
The celebrated PAC-Bayes bounds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">McAllester, 2003</a>)</cite> provide improved generalization bounds, yet do not provide a sufficient explanation of generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lotfi et al., 2022a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Livni and Moran, 2020</a>)</cite>.
A related quantity is the <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">marginal likelihood</em> of a DNN, which is connected to both PAC-Bayes bounds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Germain et al., 2016</a>)</cite> and leave-<math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-out cross-validation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fong and Holmes, 2020</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Immer et al. (2021)</a></cite> demonstrated correlation with model quality for large DNNs, although certain caveats have been reported <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lotfi et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>.
This quantity is important in SLT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Konishi and Kitagawa, 2008</a>)</cite>, since from it the Bayesian Information Criterion and Watanabe–Akaike Information Criterion can be derived.
For singular models (e.g., DNNs), the Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Watanabe, 2013</a>)</cite> was developed; it can predict quality of pre-training for downstream tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Munn and Wei, 2025</a>)</cite>.
These information criteria are derived in the regime where number of data-points <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, for fixed parameter dimension <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>; but this is no longer a valid assumption for modern deep learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Couillet and Liao, 2022</a>)</cite>.
To account for this, the Interpolating Information Criterion (IIC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>
was developed for models that attain zero-loss, although we should note that the IIC depends on an implicit regularizer for DNNs, whose full characterization remains a challenging open problem.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/free_energy_vs_acc_llm.svg" id="S1.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/537;" width="476" height="537"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S1.F1.fig3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/free_energy_vs_acc_qwen3_5.svg" id="S1.F1.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/537;" width="476" height="537"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Plots of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> versus test accuracy, for (left) <span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">torchvision</span> models trained on ImageNet-1K, (middle) Pythia models, and (right) Qwen3.5 models. Test dataset is given in brackets.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These techniques for predicting model quality are <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">data-dependent</em>, which presents multiple issues for their practical use.
Firstly, computation on massive training sets can become infeasible <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ameli et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ameli et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
Secondly, foundation models are often trained on undisclosed or proprietary datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, limiting the ability for comparisons across frontier labs.
In response, a novel line of work has considered using DNN weight matrices in isolation (<em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">data-independent</em>, i.e., without training or test data) for predicting model quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Motivation arose from the Heavy-Tailed Mechanistic Universality (HT-MU) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2020</a>)</cite> and Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization (HT-SR) theories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite>.
These related approaches are phenomenological, or semi-empirical, theories that are motivated by statistical mechanics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite>, and they are based on the empirical observation that <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spectra</em> of trained DNN weight matrices exhibit <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">heavy-tails</em>.
Metrics derived from the “heaviness” of the spectral tail are surprisingly strong predictors of model quality for both computer vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Such metrics can identify DNN layers that are “under-trained,” allowing for layer-wise learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or pruning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Motivated by this, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al. (2025)</a></cite> recently developed the High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur (HTMP) spectral distribution, which (among other things) is appropriate for modeling (heavy-tailed spectra of) weight matrices <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">after</span> training.
This probabilistic model exhibits <em id="S1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">heavy-tailed spectra</em> for weight matrices that do <span id="S1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span> necessarily possess heavy-tailed <span id="S1.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">elements</span>, a phenomenon observed in practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite>, and it can reproduce neural scaling laws for generalization error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we aim to understand—from a statistical perspective—<em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">why</em> heavy-tailed weight spectra predict model quality.
To do so, we reframe and derive certain aspects of HT-SR for DNNs using the tools of SLT and Random Matrix Theory (RMT).
Doing so will in turn allow DNN theory to more readily use and build upon the HT-SR phenomenology.
To this end, we employ a stochastic modeling framework for DNN training, and a weights and features (i.e., final activations) decomposition, to derive the marginal likelihood for <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trained features</span> <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math>. We then show that <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math> can be evaluated using only <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">final-layer weights</span>. Defining the Bayes free energy as <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}:=-\log\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}:=-\log\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>, we observe the following behavior:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p5.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="120.19" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 120.19" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,120.19) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 114.28 C 0 117.55 2.64 120.19 5.91 120.19 L 471.47 120.19 C 474.73 120.19 477.38 117.55 477.38 114.28 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 114.28 C 1.97 116.46 3.73 118.22 5.91 118.22 L 471.47 118.22 C 473.65 118.22 475.41 116.46 475.41 114.28 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:31.37em;--ltx-fo-height:6.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="92.63" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 92.63)" width="434.07"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S1.p5.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:31.37em;">
<span id="S1.p5.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">For the <span id="S1.p5.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trained</span> weights <math id="S1.p5.pic1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p5.pic1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> outputs, and correctly chosen regularization parameter <math id="S1.p5.pic1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></span>
<span id="S1.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<span id="S1.Ex1"><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" <span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span></span></span>
</span>
<span id="S1.p5.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">is strongly predictive of model quality for large-scale computer vision and language models.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate the predictive quality of this metric for many large models in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
As this metric only requires the spectrum of <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">it does not require access to training or testing data</em>, we can then explore a central question from HT-SR: <em id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">why</em> does the heaviness in the spectral tail of weight matrices predict model quality?
To answer this, we employ the HTMP distribution, with heaviness parameters <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa,\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa,\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, to derive the deterministic limit of <math id="S1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math>,
under the double-asymptotic scaling of RMT. From this quantity, we find two key spectral parameters predict model quality:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p7.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="58" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 58" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,58) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 52.09 C 0 55.36 2.64 58 5.91 58 L 471.47 58 C 474.73 58 477.38 55.36 477.38 52.09 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 52.09 C 1.97 54.27 3.73 56.03 5.91 56.03 L 471.47 56.03 C 473.65 56.03 475.41 54.27 475.41 52.09 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 33.84)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:31.37em;--ltx-fo-height:0.75em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.45em;font-size:10pt;" height="30.44" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 10.38)" width="434.07"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.p7.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:31.37em;">
<span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theoremnonumber">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem</span></span><span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Informal)<span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Under the HTMP, for fixed <math id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists an optimal ratio <math id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">κ</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">/</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math>; once this optimal ratio is achieved, <math id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#000000">ℱ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">λ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">𝐖</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly decreasing in <math id="Thmtheoremnonumberx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In a series of experiments, we observe that for large DNNs, <math id="S1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> correlates with test error very well <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">during training</span>.
In addition, for <em id="S1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trained</em> Computer Vision (CV) models, the ratio <math id="S1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math> controls underfitting / overfitting.
In contrast, <em id="S1.p8.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trained</em> LLMs attain the optimal ratio early; and increasing <math id="S1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> during training then correlates with improved performance.
These results provide a probabilistic connection between spectral properties and model quality.</p>
</div>

<figure id="S1.F2.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia-12b-deduped_pile_weight_b2m_EmbedOut_layer0_trimtop5_esd.svg" id="S1.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/87;" width="476" height="87"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The ESD (gray) and fitted <math id="S1.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution (red dotted lines), for the final-layer weights of (top) ResNet50 trained on CIFAR-100, and (bottom) Pythia-<math id="S1.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12B</annotation></semantics></math> trained on Pile.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize, in this work, we do the following:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.3em;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Derive the equivalent <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trained</span> last-layer weights formulation of the Bayes free energy of a DNN.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically demonstrate strong correlation of this free energy with model quality.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Derive the limiting free energy under HTMP, and find the minimizing HTMP parameters.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S1.I1.i4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4.</span></span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically show that training of DNNs corresponds to optimization of HTMP parameters.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S2" title="2 Related work &amp; background ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides necessary background.
In <a href="#S3" title="3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we derive <math id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> and provide an empirical evaluation.
In <a href="#S4" title="4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we find the limit of this quantity under the HTMP distribution, and we show how this quantity can be optimized; this is then connected to the training of practical DNNs.
Finally, a conclusion and discussion is given in <a href="#S5" title="5 Conclusion &amp; discussion ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
In the Appendix, we give proofs for the theoretical results, experimental details, further discussions, and further experimental and theoretical results.
Code to reproduce the experiments can be accessed <a href="https://github.com/josephwilsonmaths/heavytail.git" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">here</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related work &amp; background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RMT in deep learning.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">RMT broadly studies the limiting spectrum of matrix-valued probabilistic models. There is a long line of works that derive deterministic equivalents and generalization error for linear or random DNNs using RMT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mei and Montanari, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Atanasov et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. For a two-layer DNN, the generalization error after one gradient step was derived in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ba et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The performance of a fine-tuned DNN linearization was predicted through a Gaussian-like local spectral law <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
The limiting free energy was derived in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> for Gaussian Processes (GP) with inner-product or radial-basis kernels, and in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilson et al. (2026)</a></cite> for GPs with kernels derived from DNNs, using spectra derived from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan and Wang, 2020</a>)</cite>.
RMT for deep learning has recently been reviewed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao and Mahoney, 2026</a>)</cite>. In RMT, one considers the <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">double asymptotic limit</span>, i.e., for matrix <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{m\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{m\times n}</annotation></semantics></math>, take <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m,n\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m,n\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implicit regularization.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">explicit</em> forms of regularization for DNNs are often employed, certain aspects of a DNN such as architecture choice (e.g., depth) or optimization scheme (small-batch SGD) may <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">implicitly</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mahoney and Orecchia, 2011</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mahoney, 2012</a>)</cite> bias a DNN towards parameter values that generalize better. For homogeneous DNNs on linearly separable data, steepest descent with respect to any norm <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|</annotation></semantics></math> will implicitly minimize the parameter norm past the point of interpolation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tsilivis et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Small-batch SGD is thought to bias DNNs towards <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">flatter minima</span> during training, improving generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Keskar et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, although this idea has received criticism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dinh et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. The Geometric Complexity (GC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dherin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, defined by a discrete version of the Dirichlet Energy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jost, 2017</a>)</cite>, is a measurement of geometric smoothness that encompasses many previous notions of smoothness and seems to be correlated with model quality. A related object <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Munn and Wei, 2025</a>)</cite> is the Real Log Canonical Threshold from the Singular Learning Theory of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Watanabe (2009)</a></cite>, and its local approximation, the Local Learning Coefficient <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lau et al., 2025</a>)</cite> which also seems to correlate with model quality. We emphasize that these implicit regularization metrics depend on training data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Heavy-tailed self-regularization (HT-SR).</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">HT-SR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite> posits that the empirical spectral distributions (ESD) of trained weight matrices follow a power-law (PL) (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(u)\propto u^{-\alpha},u&gt;u_{\min},\alpha&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>min</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(u)\propto u^{-\alpha},u&gt;u_{\min},\alpha&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>), or exponentially-truncated PL (ET-PL) (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(u)\propto u^{-\alpha}e^{-\lambda u},u&gt;u_{\min},\alpha&gt;1,\lambda&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>min</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(u)\propto u^{-\alpha}e^{-\lambda u},u&gt;u_{\min},\alpha&gt;1,\lambda&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>) in the tail, due to complex correlations learnt during training, for some chosen minimum eigenvalue <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Using the fitted <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> value, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>, it was shown that for trained matrices <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}\right)=\left\{u_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>spec</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}\right)=\left\{u_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the metrics <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{\infty}^{2}=u_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{\infty}^{2}=u_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}=\alpha\log u_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}=\alpha\log u_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha}=\sum u_{i}^{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>α</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha}=\sum u_{i}^{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>, averaged over weights in a network, were strongly predictive of model-quality for CV tasks, when comparisons are made <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">within-group</span>.
HT-SR can be heuristically derived based on ideas from the statistical mechanics of learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Hinrichs, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Entropic regularization framework.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Define the stochastic minimization operation, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\smin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mo>smin</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\smin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>, with temperature <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and prior distribution <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\theta}\in\real^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}\in\real^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}:\real^{p}\to\real" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0em">:</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">→</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}:\real^{p}\to\real</annotation></semantics></math>, as</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\smin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}):=\min_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{q(\bm{\theta})}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})+\tau d_{\text{KL}}(q||\pi_{\bm{\theta}})\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>smin</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\smin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}):=\min_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{q(\bm{\theta})}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})+\tau d_{\text{KL}}(q||\pi_{\bm{\theta}})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of probability distributions on the support of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote the minimizing density over parameters as <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\theta)=\argsmin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0.1389em">argsmin</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\theta)=\argsmin_{\bm{\theta}}^{\pi_{\bm{\theta}},\tau}\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>, provided it exists and is unique. Such probabilistic frameworks of training have been considered previously <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sonthalia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Note that <a href="#S2.E1" title="In Entropic regularization framework. ‣ 2 Related work &amp; background ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> optimizes a PAC-Bayes bound on the test-error when <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is the training loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2025</a>, Appendix B.)</cite>, and it is related to the variational inference performed during stochastic gradient descent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chaudhari and Soatto, 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Free energy for trained weights</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first derive <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math>, the negative log-marginal for interpolating <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trained features</span>, that can be evaluated using only trained <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">final-layer weights</span>. We then show that this quantity correlates very well with model quality for many large DNNs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Notation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a DNN <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bf f}:\real^{d}\times\real^{p}\to\real^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0em">:</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">×</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}:\real^{d}\times\real^{p}\to\real^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, for inputs <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bf x}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\real^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf x}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\real^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> and parameters <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{\theta}\in\bm{\Theta}\subseteq\real^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝚯</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}\in\bm{\Theta}\subseteq\real^{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We take training dataset <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\left\{{\bf x}_{i},{\bf y}_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\left\{{\bf x}_{i},{\bf y}_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\real^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒴</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\real^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, and loss function <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We denote the concatenations of training data as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{X}}=[{\bf x}_{1}|\dots|{\bf x}_{n}]^{T}\in\real^{n\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{X}}=[{\bf x}_{1}|\dots|{\bf x}_{n}]^{T}\in\real^{n\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{Y}}=[{\bf y}_{1}|\dots|{\bf y}_{n}]^{T}\in\real^{n\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐘</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{Y}}=[{\bf y}_{1}|\dots|{\bf y}_{n}]^{T}\in\real^{n\times m}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In our setting, it will be useful to consider a decomposition of a DNN into its <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">non-linear features</span> and <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">final-layer weights</span>. We denote the function space of features as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math>; then we write <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bf f}:\real^{d}\times\real^{d_{L}\times m}\times\mathcal{F}\to\real^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0em">:</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">×</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}:\real^{d}\times\real^{d_{L}\times m}\times\mathcal{F}\to\real^{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, for inputs <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bf x}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\real^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf x}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\real^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, final-layer weights <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}\in\real^{d_{L}\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}\in\real^{d_{L}\times m}</annotation></semantics></math>, and feature function <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi\in\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi\in\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math>. The functional form of the DNN is <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf f}({\bf x};{\mathbf{W}},\phi)=\phi({\bf x})^{T}{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}({\bf x};{\mathbf{W}},\phi)=\phi({\bf x})^{T}{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We can represent the function evaluated on training inputs <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{X}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐗</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{X}}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf f}({\mathbf{X}};{\mathbf{W}},\phi)=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}({\mathbf{X}};{\mathbf{W}},\phi)=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is the concatenation <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m18" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Phi=[\phi({\bf x}_{1})|\dots|\phi({\bf x}_{n})]^{T}\in\real^{n\times d_{L}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi=[\phi({\bf x}_{1})|\dots|\phi({\bf x}_{n})]^{T}\in\real^{n\times d_{L}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote the matrix-normal distribution by <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m19" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(.,.,.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(.,.,.)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Optimal features under interpolation for ridge regression</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The exact training dynamics of large DNNs are highly complex, prohibiting careful analysis. To simplify analysis, we consider training <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, using the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">entropic regularization</span> framework in <a href="#S2.E1" title="In Entropic regularization framework. ‣ 2 Related work &amp; background ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, for loss function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}=\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d_{L}},\text{I}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}=\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d_{L}},\text{I}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math>. Under this framework, optimal <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">feature</span> density <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle q(\Phi)=\argsmin_{\Phi}^{\pi_{\Phi},\eta}\smin_{{\mathbf{W}}}^{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}},\tau}\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0.1389em">argsmin</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0.167em">smin</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle q(\Phi)=\argsmin_{\Phi}^{\pi_{\Phi},\eta}\smin_{{\mathbf{W}}}^{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}},\tau}\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{W}},\Phi),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">provided the minimum exists and is unique. By <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al. (2025, Proposition 3.1)</a></cite>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\Phi)\propto\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)^{\tau/\eta}\pi_{\Phi}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\Phi)\propto\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)^{\tau/\eta}\pi_{\Phi}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math> is the marginal (Gibbs) likelihood with prior <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)\propto{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∝</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub></msub><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}_{\tau}(\Phi)\propto{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>.
So, we observe that trained features concentrate around regions with high marginal likelihood.
Under our loss function and prior, we can explicitly compute (calculations are given in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Derivation of feature marginal likelihood for ridge-regression ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>) the negative log marginal for the trained features (i.e., Bayes Free Energy):</p>
<table id="S3.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{1}{nm}\mathcal{F}^{\tau_{m},\lambda_{m}}_{n}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{1}{nm}\mathcal{F}^{\tau_{m},\lambda_{m}}_{n}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐘</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
