</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{K}}_{\lambda_{m},\tau_{m}}=\Phi\Phi^{T}+\lambda_{m}\tau_{m}/2\text{I}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{K}}_{\lambda_{m},\tau_{m}}=\Phi\Phi^{T}+\lambda_{m}\tau_{m}/2\text{I}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{m}=1/(m\sigma^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{m}=1/(m\sigma^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{m}=\tau m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{m}=\tau m</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained</span> features <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>, the Bayes Free Energy can be used to measure model quality; while this is not novel, the following extension is: under certain assumptions, for training temperature <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the Bayes Free Energy for well-trained features can be evaluated using <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">only</span> the final-layer weights <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, up to some additive terms that cancel when comparing Bayes Free Energy between models trained on the same dataset.
Taking <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> concentrates the marginal likelihood on the sub-manifold of interpolators; this concentration approach was used to derive the IIC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023c</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 1</span></span><span id="Thmassumption1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Interpolation)<span id="Thmassumption1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For <span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained</span> features <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>, assume <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq m,d_{L}&gt;m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq m,d_{L}&gt;m</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{Rank}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Rank}}({\mathbf{Y}})=m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{Rank}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Rank}}({\mathbf{Y}})=m</annotation></semantics></math>. Further, assume that <span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained</span> weights are given by <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and that <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi{\mathbf{W}}={\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi{\mathbf{W}}={\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This minimum-norm interpolating solution <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math> is key; <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains all necessary information about the relationship between features and targets. These assumptions have strong motivations: under our entropic regularization training framework, taking <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau,\sigma^{2}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau,\sigma^{2}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau/\sigma^{2}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau/\sigma^{2}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> ensures <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}\to\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}\to\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the same result applies in the deterministic optimization setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Golub and Pereyra, 1973</a>)</cite>.
Further, in a sufficiently over-parameterized multiclass logistic regression setting, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2021)</a></cite> show trained weights “interpolate” the centered training outputs.
Under neural collapse assumptions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papyan et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, these results extend to over-parameterized neural networks.
Using this interpolating relationship, we can now evaluate <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Optimal features under interpolation for ridge regression ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> using only the final-layer weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Define <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma:={\mathbf{Y}}^{T}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐘</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma:={\mathbf{Y}}^{T}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, under <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1 (Interpolation). ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, as <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{F}^{\lambda_{m},\tau_{m}}_{n}(\Phi)}{nm}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{F}^{\lambda_{m},\tau_{m}}_{n}(\Phi)}{nm}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{{\textnormal{Tr}}(\lambda_{m}{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})}{2n}-\frac{\log\det\left(\lambda_{m}{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}\right)}{2n}+\frac{\log(\pi\tau)^{n-m}}{2n}+\frac{\log\det 2\pi\Sigma/m}{2n}+\mathcal{O}(\tau)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">det</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>λ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><mi>𝐖</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">det</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{{\textnormal{Tr}}(\lambda_{m}{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})}{2n}-\frac{\log\det\left(\lambda_{m}{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}\right)}{2n}+\frac{\log(\pi\tau)^{n-m}}{2n}+\frac{\log\det 2\pi\Sigma/m}{2n}+\mathcal{O}(\tau).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of this theorem is given in <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Derivation of BFE-W ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.
We observe that the final three terms will cancel as <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> when comparing models trained on the same dataset. Dropping the dependence of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> on m, dropping the constant terms that cancel (except for a Gaussian entropy term), and correctly normalizing the trace and log-determinant terms, we arrive at the <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">relative free energy</span>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS2.p4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="32.05" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 32.05" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,32.05) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 26.14 C 0 29.41 2.64 32.05 5.91 32.05 L 471.47 32.05 C 474.73 32.05 477.38 29.41 477.38 26.14 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 26.14 C 1.97 28.32 3.73 30.08 5.91 30.08 L 471.47 30.08 C 473.65 30.08 475.41 28.32 475.41 26.14 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 18.27)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:31.37em;--ltx-fo-height:0em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.32em;font-size:10pt;" height="4.49" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)" width="434.07"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

<span class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m4" class="ltx_Math" <span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span>
<span rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(BFE-<math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span></span></span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, we have derived, under an entropic regularization framework, a data-free metric that directly measures model quality of the underlying DNN features. We see that <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> involves a trade-off between <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{-1}\log\det{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">det</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{-1}\log\det{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, controlled by parameter <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> (prior scale). The advantage of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> over <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Optimal features under interpolation for ridge regression ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for comparing models is immediate: <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> does <em id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> require access to training or validation data, and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math> is often of a <em id="S3.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">much</em> smaller size than <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Note that when <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m&gt;d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m&gt;d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math> is rank-deficient.
In practice, one might add a small ridge-parameter <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> for <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>, i.e., <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}+\epsilon\text{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>I</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}+\epsilon\text{I}</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, one can also derive a dual formulation of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>, to obtain:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{d_{L}}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}}):=\frac{\lambda}{2d_{L}}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}{\mathbf{W}}^{T})-\frac{1}{2d_{L}}\log\det{\mathbf{W}}{\mathbf{W}}^{T}+\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}." <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">The full asymptotic expansion is given along with its derivation in <a href="#Thmlemma2" title="Lemma 2. ‣ B.2 Dual form ‣ Appendix B Derivation of BFE-W ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Dual form ‣ Appendix B Derivation of BFE-W ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>. While this free energy does not immediately allow for comparison between models with differing <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, we will see that it still correlates surprisingly well with model quality, across models with differing <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmremark1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmremark1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 1</span></span><span id="Thmremark1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmremark1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmremark1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmremark1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">To ensure <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> correlates with the posterior predictive loss, one can set <math id="Thmremark1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=\argmin_{\lambda}\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mi>λ</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=\argmin_{\lambda}\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda}({\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lotfi et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">MacKay, 1992</a>)</cite>. Taking a derivative immediately gives <math id="Thmremark1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=m/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=m/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Interestingly, at this scale,</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda^{*}}({\mathbf{W}})=\frac{1+\log 2\pi}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})}{\det({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})^{1/m}}\right)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{m}^{\lambda^{*}}({\mathbf{W}})=\frac{1+\log 2\pi}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})}{\det({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})^{1/m}}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmremark1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmremark1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hence, at the optimal regularizer, the free energy is measuring the log-ratio of the arithmetic spectral mean versus geometric spectral mean.
This is trivially minimized at <math id="Thmremark1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}\propto{\mathbf{U}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∝</mo><mi>𝐔</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}\propto{\mathbf{U}}</annotation></semantics></math> (up to a scalar multiple), where <math id="Thmremark1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{U}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐔</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{U}}</annotation></semantics></math> has orthonormal columns; this corresponds to the case when <math id="Thmremark1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi\Phi^{T}\propto{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathbf{Y}}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>𝐘𝐘</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi\Phi^{T}\propto{\mathbf{Y}}{\mathbf{Y}}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Outside of this “optimal-learning scenario,” behavior is non-trivial.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Empirical evaluation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we empirically demonstrate the correlation of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> with model quality.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computer vision (CV).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We take a large number of high-performing models, across different architecture types (e.g., ResNet, DenseNet etc.) from the <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">torchvision</span> model zoo that have been pretrained on ImageNet-1K, where test accuracy and model weights are provided. We set <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=m/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=m/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> for each model. In <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (left), we present <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> versus top-5 test accuracy, where we see a strong Spearman correlation of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=-0.71}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.71</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=-0.71}</annotation></semantics></math> across groups<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              There is also strong correlation within groups.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Large language models (LLMs).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ both the Pythia project <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> models (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="410" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>410</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">410</annotation></semantics></math>M, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.8</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.9</annotation></semantics></math>B, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math>B), as well as the Qwen3.5 suite <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026</a>)</cite> (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="35" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>35</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35</annotation></semantics></math>B, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="122" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>122</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">122</annotation></semantics></math>B, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="397" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>397</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">397</annotation></semantics></math>B). In <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (middle) we compare the dual <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> against LAMBADA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paperno et al., 2016</a>)</cite> test accuracy for the Pythia models, where we see a solid correlation of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=-0.66}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.66</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=-0.66}</annotation></semantics></math>. In <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right), we repeat this for the Qwen3.5 models, using the MMLU-Pro benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>; here we see a stronger correlation of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=-0.77}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.77</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=-0.77}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is strong evidence that for both CV models and LLMs, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> is, perhaps surprisingly, strongly predictive of model quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare against the HT-SR metrics in <a href="#A9.SS1" title="I.1 Comparison to HT-SR metrics ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I.1</span></a> for the CV models, where <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> shows much stronger correlation. Note that for CV, two model classes did not show correlation between <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and accuracy.
Firstly, models that used <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">dropout</span> before the final-layer weight did not show correlation, as dropout prevents complex correlations from occurring in final-layer weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.
Secondly, vision transformers did not show correlation.
This could be because division of vision transformers at the last-layer into <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">features</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weights</span> may be too crude.
See <a href="#A9.SS2" title="I.2 When last-layer free energy does not predict model quality ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I.2</span></a> for results showing this (alongside HT-SR metrics, which perform as poorly).
The extension to such models is left for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Heavy-tails and free energy</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the previous section, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> was derived for the final-layer weights.
In this section, we will relax this condition, and consider <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for all weights of a DNN.
We will observe in the sequel that <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for deeper DNN weights can still correlate very well with model quality, and we will give theoretical motivation (in <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Motivation for application of BFE-W for deeper layer weights ‣ Appendix F Further details ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>).
Thus, equipped with a metric, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>, that explicitly connects trained weights of a DNN to model quality, we will use the machinery of RMT to investigate the question of why—from a statistical perspective—the spectral shape of heavy-tailed weights is so strongly predictive of model performance.
We give details on the spectral shape of <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained weights</span>; we then use this to analyze how <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> is optimized for certain spectral parameters, under an RMT limit; and we conclude with empirical validation for large-scale DNNs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F3.fig3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia-1b-deduped_pile_weight_b2m_EmbedOut_layer0_trimtop5_weight_inverse_test_loss_vs_free_energy_vs_epochs.svg" id="S4.F3.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/271;" width="476" height="271"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F3.fig4" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia-12b-deduped_pile_weight_b2m_EmbedOut_layer0_trimtop5_weight_inverse_test_loss_vs_free_energy_vs_epochs.svg" id="S4.F3.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/271;" width="476" height="271"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Test CE, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and <math id="S4.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math>, vs. epochs. Model quality during training is highly correlated with BFE. Further, <math id="S4.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math> closely approximates <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Trained weight spectra</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The spectrum of weight matrices before and after training differs substantially <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite>. The ESD of weight matrices <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{t}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{t}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, for DNNs at <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">initialization<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">2</span></span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <span id="footnote2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">Under the standard initialization schemes for DNNs (e.g., Xavier, He, Glorot initializations).</span></span></span></span></span> converges<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            As <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{l},d_{l-1}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{l},d_{l-1}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="footnote3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{l}/d_{l-1}\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{l}/d_{l-1}\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span> to the Marchenko-Pastur distribution (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{MP}_{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">MP</mtext><mi>γ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{MP}_{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math>), with aspect ratio <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=d_{l}/d_{l-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=d_{l}/d_{l-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. After training, the spectrum of weight matrices is often well-modeled by the HTMP distribution (see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al. (2025, Proposition 5.3)</a></cite>), which admits heavy-tails.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 2</span></span><span id="Thmassumption2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., Convolutional, Dense, etc.) in a DNN, in the limit as <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{l},d_{l-1}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{l},d_{l-1}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{l}/d_{l-1}\to\gamma\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{l}/d_{l-1}\to\gamma\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>, the spectral distribution of <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau(d_{l})\text{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">I</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau(d_{l})\text{I}</annotation></semantics></math> converges weakly in probability to the <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution, where <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min{\textnormal{spec}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l})=:\tau(d_{l})\to\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mtext>spec</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min{\textnormal{spec}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l})=:\tau(d_{l})\to\tau</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmdefinition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmdefinition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmdefinition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmdefinition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmdefinition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau\text{I}\right)\sim\mathbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>spec</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">I</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>𝐇𝐓𝐌𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau\text{I}\right)\sim\mathbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="Thmdefinition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\right)\sim\mathbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>spec</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>𝐇𝐓𝐌𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{spec}}\left({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\right)\sim\mathbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">See <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for empirical validation of this assumption for large DNNs. We provide further details on the <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur distribution ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, as well as some mild integrability assumptions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Limiting free energy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now find the deterministic limit of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> under RMT scaling. This quantity will allow us to connect spectral shape qualities of trained weights to model quality, through the empirically observed correlation between <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and model quality in <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Empirical evaluation ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Trained weight spectra ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption4" title="Assumption 4 (Uniform Integrability). ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and <a href="#Thmassumption5" title="Assumption 5 (Logarithmic Integrability). ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>,</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U(a,b;z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U(a,b;z)</annotation></semantics></math> is the Tricomi confluent hypergeometric function.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is found in <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Proof of Theorem 2. ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>. Now, this deterministic limit depends non-trivially on several parameters.
Hence, we would like to find a parameter combination through which analysis is simplified.
To this end, and to investigate the question of why heavier-tails correspond to improved model quality, note that the density <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\rho}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ρ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\rho}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> follows</p>
<table id="S4.EGx10" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}(x)\propto x^{\frac{\kappa}{2\gamma}-1+\frac{\kappa}{2}}e^{-\beta x},\quad x\to\infty." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>ρ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}(x)\propto x^{\frac{\kappa}{2\gamma}-1+\frac{\kappa}{2}}e^{-\beta x},\quad x\to\infty.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Hence, under <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>, either increasing <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> or decreasing <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> (while keeping the other parameter fixed) will give <span id="S4.SS2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">heavier</span> tails. A natural quantity to consider is therefore the scale-based heaviness <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\kappa)=\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\kappa)=\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math>. We now present a result which states that there exists, under certain assumptions, an optimal scale-based heaviness <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>; once this optimal <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is achieved, increasing <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> will decrease the limiting free energy. The proof is given in <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Proof of Theorem 3. ‣ Appendix E Proofs for convexity and optimality of free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#S4.E3" title="In Theorem 2. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we have the following results:</span></p>
<dl id="S4.I1" class="ltx_description">
<dt id="S4.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a.</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For fixed </span><math id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, the first moment </span><math id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{1}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> and the Shannon transform </span><math id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}_{\rho}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mi>ρ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}_{\rho}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> (defined in </span><a href="#Thmdefinition2" title="Definition 2. ‣ D.1 Shannon transform ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Definition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">) are both increasing in </span><math id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\kappa)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\kappa)</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S4.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">b.</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For fixed </span><math id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;0" display="inline" stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, </span><math id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}(\kappa)=2\gamma/\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}(\kappa)=2\gamma/\lambda</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> for which </span><math id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> reaches its minimum.</span></p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="S4.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="S4.I1.ix3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">c.</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="S4.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For </span><math id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, at </span><math id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=\beta^{*}(\kappa)=\lambda\kappa/2\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=\beta^{*}(\kappa)=\lambda\kappa/2\gamma</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">, </span><math id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> is strictly decreasing in </span><math id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Under <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 4.1 Trained weight spectra ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption4" title="Assumption 4 (Uniform Integrability). ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#Thmassumption5" title="Assumption 5 (Logarithmic Integrability). ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we see that the competing terms in <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> are increasing and decreasing, respectively, with <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, due to the following identities:</p>
