rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mo mathsize="0.700em">ℙ</mo></mover><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lim_{d_{l-1},d_{l}\to\infty}\frac{1}{d_{l}}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l})\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\to}\mu_{1},\quad\lim_{d_{l-1},d_{l}\to\infty}\frac{1}{d_{l}}\log\det({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l})\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\to}\lim_{x\to 0}(\mathcal{V}(x)+\log(x)).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">In practice, the spectral gap is non-zero, and hence we must impose further assumptions on the parameterization of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. We see in <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Using HTMP to understand training dynamics ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> that for CV models, <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> are approximately inversely proportional over training epochs; under this assumption, we have the following lemma, whose proof is given in <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Proof of Lemma 1. ‣ Appendix E Proofs for convexity and optimality of free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmlemma1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlemma1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 1</span></span><span id="Thmlemma1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlemma1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlemma1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlemma1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>, if <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=c/\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=c/\tau</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}(\kappa)=2\gamma\kappa/\lambda(\kappa+2\gamma c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}(\kappa)=2\gamma\kappa/\lambda(\kappa+2\gamma c)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Using HTMP to understand training dynamics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now employ the theoretical results above to explain learning dynamics for large DNNs. Further experimental results can be found in <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia_resnet_htmp_parameters.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/130;" width="476" height="130"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fitted <math id="S4.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters at each epoch, for ResNet50 (trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), Pythia-1B and Pythia-12B models. All weights are final-layer weights, except for ResNet50 CIFAR-10, where flattened convolutional weight at the third layer is used.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">CV.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider ResNet50, trained on both CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10, for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>200</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200</annotation></semantics></math> epochs. After reaching zero training loss (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy is reached at epoch <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>25</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25</annotation></semantics></math> respectively), each training epoch corresponds to a new <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trained</span> model. In <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(top) we plot the test cross-entropy versus <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math>, for the final-layer weights (CIFAR-100) and the flattened convolutional weight at the third layer (CIFAR-10, due to small dimension of final weights). We take <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is the epoch when test error is minimized. Interestingly, taking <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> at each epoch <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> gives poor correlation for these CV models (see <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Choice of precision parameter 𝜆 ‣ Appendix F Further details ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a> for an in-depth discussion about the choice of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>). Using <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=d_{l}/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=d_{l}/{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}})</annotation></semantics></math>, we observe that <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math> very closely follow the test error curve, with correlations of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=0.927}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.927</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=0.927}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=0.984}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.984</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=0.984}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Using HTMP to understand training dynamics ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (left), <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> stays mostly fixed for each model, while <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}=\kappa_{t}/\beta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}=\kappa_{t}/\beta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> decreases during training epochs <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. In <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we plot test error, and the empirical and asymptotic free energy, against <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>. We plot the optimal ratio <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> from <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and observe that the minimum test error occurs when <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}=h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}=h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is directly measuring the level of underfitting / overfitting of the model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We repeat this process for the Pythia-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>B and Pythia-<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math>B models, trained on Pile. We plot the empirical and asymptotic free energies using the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">EmbedOut</span> weights of the model (final-connected weights). We plot the free energy against the cross-entropy for the OpenAI curated LAMBADA test dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paperno et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. We compute <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> using the same process as for the CV models above. We see again that we have very close adherence of the free energies with the test error, with correlations of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=0.986}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.986</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=0.986}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=0.965}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.965</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=0.965}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. Note that in all figures, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">epochs</span> of training for Pythia models refers to <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">steps</span> of training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The spectral behaviour of these LLMs contrasts that of the CV models; in <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Using HTMP to understand training dynamics ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (middle, right), we observe that <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> follows very closely the optimal <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{*}(\kappa_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{*}(\kappa_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> from <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (remembering that <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}(\kappa)=\kappa/\beta^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}(\kappa)=\kappa/\beta^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>), while <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> increases during training. As predicted in <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for small <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we see in <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (bottom) that this increase in <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> results in a decreasing free energy, which correlates with a decrease in test error. This dual optimization is distinct from the training dynamics for CV models, suggesting an inherent difference in learning dynamics.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion &amp; discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">HT-SR theory posits that the spectral distributions of DNN weight matrices can predict model quality.
In this work, we validate this claim through a probabilistic framework; we derive a data-free metric, the Bayes Free Energy evaluated using only the final-layer weights, and we empirically show that this metric is strongly predictive of model quality, for both CV models and LLMs.
To understand <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">why</em> heavy-tailed weight matrices may generalize better,
we derive the deterministic limiting quantity of this metric under the assumption that weight spectra follow the recently proposed
<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution.
We then show that this free energy is convex in the scale-based heaviness parameter, <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, and that an optimal parameter <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> exists. Once this optimal parameter is attained, we show increasing <math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> monotonically decreases free energy (correlating with improved model quality). We empirically find that CV model training correlates with optimizing <math id="S5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>; in contrast, LLM models optimize <math id="S5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> early, and instead increasing <math id="S5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> correlates with improved performance. Thus, we provide results that mirror the findings of the HT-SR theory; that optimal model quality can be observed in the shape of weight spectra.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations &amp; future work.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">There are several limitations of our work; some of these limitations present clear paths for future work. Firstly, we note that <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> was only derived for final-layer weights, and for regression. Further, the dual formulation of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> cannot immediately be compared across models with different activation dimension <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>. Providing a remedy to these limitations is a promising avenue for future work. Further work could also involve extending <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> to models that use Dropout before the final-layer, or Vision Transformer models, as these models did not show correlation between <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and model quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also note that a limitation of our framework is that for CV models during training, the prior precision parameter <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> must be tuned post-hoc to optimize correlation. Deriving <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> a-priori would allow one to measure <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters during training, and to early-stop when <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}\approx h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}\approx h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Further future work should also involve attempting to theoretically derive the <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters for certain classes of DNNs, or to show how certain training mechanisms affect these spectral parameters. Our framework would then elucidate how these mechanisms optimize model quality, through the free energy connection.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<li id="bib.bib30" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_article"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Dherin <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2022)</span>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix" style="font-size:144%;">Appendices</h2>

</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Derivation of feature marginal likelihood for ridge-regression</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first derive the marginal (Gibbs) likelihood for features <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>, under the training framework detailed in <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Optimal features under interpolation for ridge regression ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>. We then provide the Bayes Free Energy, which is the negative log of the marginal likelihood.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Marginal likelihood derivation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The marginal (Gibbs) likelihood in this setting is given by <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub></msub><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>, for loss function <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}=\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d_{L}},\text{I}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}=\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d_{L}},\text{I}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math>. As <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math> is only defined up to constants of proportionality, we redefine the marginal likelihood as</p>
<table id="A1.EGx12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex9"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)=(\pi\tau)^{-nm/2}{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub></msub><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)=(\pi\tau)^{-nm/2}{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}\exp(-L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)/\tau).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This will simplify the calculations.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmremark2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmremark2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 2</span></span><span id="Thmremark2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmremark2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmremark2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmremark2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The marginal (Gibbs) likelihood for this ridge-regression setting was derived in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al. (2025)</a></cite>; however, we provide a different derivation, using integrals of matrix-normals. Further, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al. (2025)</a></cite> provides the derivation of <math id="Thmremark2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Thmremark2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}+\mu||{\mathbf{W}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L({\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}+\mu||{\mathbf{W}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We take <math id="Thmremark2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Now, note that <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(\pi\tau)^{-nm/2}\exp(-||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}/\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">−</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐘</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em">/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\pi\tau)^{-nm/2}\exp(-||\Phi{\mathbf{W}}-{\mathbf{Y}}||_{F}^{2}/\tau)</annotation></semantics></math> is the likelihood of the model <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{Y}}|{\mathbf{W}},\Phi\sim\mathcal{N}(\Phi{\mathbf{W}},\tau/2\text{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐘</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>I</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{Y}}|{\mathbf{W}},\Phi\sim\mathcal{N}(\Phi{\mathbf{W}},\tau/2\text{I})</annotation></semantics></math>. Then,</p>
<table id="A1.EGx13" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex10"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}}}p({\mathbf{Y}}|{\mathbf{W}},\Phi)=\int_{{\textnormal{supp}}(\pi_{{\mathbf{W}}})}p({\mathbf{Y}}|{\mathbf{W}},\Phi)p({\mathbf{W}})d{\mathbf{W}}=p({\mathbf{Y}}|\Phi)." stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝐖</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐘</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐘</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We can write the model as <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{Y}}=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}+\bm{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐘</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{Y}}=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}+\bm{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d},\text{I}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\text{I}_{d},\text{I}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\tau/2\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\tau/2\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math>. The sum of matrix normals is a matrix normal, and we are integrating out <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, using standard matrix-normal properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gupta and Nagar, 1999</a>)</cite>,</p>
<table id="A1.EGx14" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle{\mathbf{Y}}=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}+\epsilon\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\Phi\Phi^{T}+\tau/2\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{m})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐘</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle{\mathbf{Y}}=\Phi{\mathbf{W}}+\epsilon\sim\mathcal{M}\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^{2}\Phi\Phi^{T}+\tau/2\text{I}_{n},\text{I}_{m}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Therefore,</p>

rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>τ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-nm/2}\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}{\textnormal{Tr}}\left({\mathbf{Y}}^{T}\left(\Phi\Phi^{T}+\frac{\tau}{2\sigma^{2}}\text{I}_{n}\right)^{-1}{\mathbf{Y}}\right)\right)}{\det\left(\Phi\Phi^{T}+\frac{\tau}{2\sigma^{2}}\text{I}_{n}\right)^{m/2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Bayes free energy for regression</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define the Bayes Free Energy as the negative log of the marginal likelihood, i.e., <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi):=-\log\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi):=-\log\mathcal{Z}^{\tau}_{n}(\Phi)</annotation></semantics></math>. Taking <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{m}=1/m\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{m}=1/m\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{m}=\tau m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{m}=\tau m</annotation></semantics></math>, we can compute that</p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Derivation of BFE-W</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we first prove <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, and then derive the dual formulation. To prove these results, we rely on asymptotic expansions of <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{Tr}}((A+\nu\text{I})^{-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>I</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{Tr}}((A+\nu\text{I})^{-1})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\log\det(A+\nu\text{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ν</mi><mtext>I</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\det(A+\nu\text{I})</annotation></semantics></math>, for singular matrix <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and perturbative parameter <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu\ll 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>≪</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu\ll 1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Primal form</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof of <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</h6>
<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Under our rank assumptions and interpolation assumptions, <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi={\mathbf{Y}}{\mathbf{W}}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐘𝐖</mi><mo>†</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi={\mathbf{Y}}{\mathbf{W}}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu=\lambda_{m}\tau_{m}/2=\tau/2\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu=\lambda_{m}\tau_{m}/2=\tau/2\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We consider the trace and log-determinant terms in <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3.1 Optimal features under interpolation for ridge regression ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> separately.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">For the <span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trace term</span>, for <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu\ll 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>≪</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu\ll 1</annotation></semantics></math>, we get the following singular asymptotic expansion around <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> for positive semi-definite <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2015</a>)</cite>,</span></p>
<table id="A2.EGx17" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.Ex16"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle({\mathbf{A}}+\nu\text{I})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\nu}(\text{I}-{\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger})+{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger}+\mathcal{O(\nu)}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>I</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>ν</mi></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>I</mtext><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐀𝐀</mi><mo>†</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ν</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle({\mathbf{A}}+\nu\text{I})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\nu}(\text{I}-{\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger})+{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger}+\mathcal{O(\nu)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">Noting that <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\text{I}-{\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>I</mtext><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐀𝐀</mi><mo>†</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\text{I}-{\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger})</annotation></semantics></math> is a projection onto the kernel of <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{A}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{A}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and noting that <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{Y}}\in{\textnormal{Range}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Range}}(\Phi\Phi^{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐘</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mtext>Range</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Range</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{Y}}\in{\textnormal{Range}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Range}}(\Phi\Phi^{T})</annotation></semantics></math>, we get that</span></p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex17.m1" class="ltx_Math" </div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">For the <span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">log-determinant term</span>, using the Weinstein-Aronszajn identity: for <math id="A2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{n\times m},{\mathbf{B}}\in\real^{m\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo rspace="0em">∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{n\times m},{\mathbf{B}}\in\real^{m\times n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\det({\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{B}}+\nu\text{I}_{n})=\nu^{n-m}\det({\mathbf{B}}{\mathbf{A}}+\nu\text{I}_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐀𝐁</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ν</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐁𝐀</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>I</mtext><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det({\mathbf{A}}{\mathbf{B}}+\nu\text{I}_{n})=\nu^{n-m}\det({\mathbf{B}}{\mathbf{A}}+\nu\text{I}_{m})</annotation></semantics></math>. and the Taylor expansion of the log-determinant of an invertible matrix around <span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">I</span>, we see that</span></p>

</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Dual form</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m&gt;d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m&gt;d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, then <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1 (Interpolation). ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is invalid. Instead, we take the following, very similar, set of assumptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 3</span></span><span id="Thmassumption3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Dual Interpolation)<span id="Thmassumption3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For <span id="Thmassumption3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained</span> features <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>, assume <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq m,m&gt;d_{L}\geq c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq m,m&gt;d_{L}\geq c</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{Rank}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Rank}}({\mathbf{Y}})=c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐘</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{Rank}}(\Phi)={\textnormal{Rank}}({\mathbf{Y}})=c</annotation></semantics></math>. Further, assume that <span id="Thmassumption3.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">trained</span> weights are given by <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>†</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}=\Phi^{\dagger}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and that <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi{\mathbf{W}}={\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi{\mathbf{W}}={\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that we allow for rank <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\leq d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\leq d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, to allow for comparison across different models, with different <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>. This point will be expanded upon later. We then have the following lemma, whose statement and proof follows very closely that of <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmlemma2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlemma2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 2</span></span><span id="Thmlemma2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlemma2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlemma2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlemma2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Define <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma:={\mathbf{Y}}^{T}{\mathbf{Y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐘</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐘</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma:={\mathbf{Y}}^{T}{\mathbf{Y}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, under <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3 (Dual Interpolation). ‣ B.2 Dual form ‣ Appendix B Derivation of BFE-W ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Assumption</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, as <math id="Thmlemma2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\to 0^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\to 0^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
