<p id="A5.SS4.p2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS4.p2.4.1" class="ltx_text">Hence,</span></p>
<table id="A5.EGx73" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A5.Ex89"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A5.Ex89.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A5.Ex89.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}(1+d_{1}z^{-1}+d_{2}z^{-2}+\cdots)(1-c_{1}z^{-1}+(c_{1}^{2}-c_{2})z^{-2}+\cdots)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}(1+d_{1}z^{-1}+d_{2}z^{-2}+\cdots)(1-c_{1}z^{-1}+(c_{1}^{2}-c_{2})z^{-2}+\cdots)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A5.Ex90"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A5.Ex90.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}+(d_{1}-c_{1})z^{-2}+((c_{1}^{2}-c_{2})-c_{1}d_{1}+d_{2})z^{-3}+\mathcal{O}(z^{-4})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}+(d_{1}-c_{1})z^{-2}+((c_{1}^{2}-c_{2})-c_{1}d_{1}+d_{2})z^{-3}+\mathcal{O}(z^{-4})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A5.Ex91"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A5.Ex91.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}-(a-b+1)z^{-2}+(a-b+1)(2a-b+2)z^{-3}+\mathcal{O}(z^{-4})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim z^{-1}-(a-b+1)z^{-2}+(a-b+1)(2a-b+2)z^{-3}+\mathcal{O}(z^{-4}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS4.p2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS4.p2.5.1" class="ltx_text">For the negative case, we note that <math id="A5.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U(a,b,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U(a,b,z)</annotation></semantics></math> has a branch cut on the real-negative axis. However, we can write <math id="A5.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-z=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}ze^{i(\pi-\epsilon)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-z=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}ze^{i(\pi-\epsilon)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Substituting this into the above asymptotic expansion</span></p>
<table id="A5.EGx74" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A5.Ex92"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A5.Ex92.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle U(a,b,-z)\sim z^{-a}e^{-i\pi a}\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_{s}(a-b+1)_{s}}{s!}z^{-s}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle U(a,b,-z)\sim z^{-a}e^{-i\pi a}\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_{s}(a-b+1)_{s}}{s!}z^{-s}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS4.p2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS4.p2.6.1" class="ltx_text">The negative factors will cancel in numerator and denominator of <math id="A5.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>, except for a single negative multiplicative factor (arising from exponent of <math id="A5.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a+1</annotation></semantics></math>). Hence, we have the result.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Further details</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide further theoretical and experimental details which we could not include in the main body.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Connection of BFE-W to previous implicit regularization metrics</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand why <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> correlates so strongly with model quality, we can understand its connection to previous measurements of implicit regularization.
Firstly, <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>Tr</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{-1}{\textnormal{Tr}}({\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}})</annotation></semantics></math> is an HT-SR weight metric. This term also provides a connection to the Geometric Complexity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dherin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>; and this term is implicitly regularized after interpolation for gradient flow training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tsilivis et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Secondly, while the log-determinant is less common in the literature, a key term in the IIC is <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{-1}\log\det\left({\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}~{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}^{T}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">det</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐃𝐟</mi><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐃𝐟</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{-1}\log\det\left({\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}~{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}^{T}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}~{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃𝐟</mi><mo lspace="0.330em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐃𝐟</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}~{\mathbf{D}}{\bf f}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacot et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. This measures the complexity of <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}</annotation></semantics></math> through the volume of the distribution of functions induced by parameter Jacobian of <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf f}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf f}</annotation></semantics></math>. The second term in <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> instead measures the volume of functions induced by the last-layer weights, i.e., a <span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">functional complexity</span>, and is the information gain for a Gaussian model with kernel <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Motivation for application of BFE-W for deeper layer weights</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> was derived for final-layer weights, we can motivate the use for weights from deeper layers. Specifically, for deeper weights <math id="A6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> corresponds to the Bayes free energy for an auxiliary Gaussian Process with precision matrix <math id="A6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{K}}=\lambda{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐊</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{K}}=\lambda{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, for artificial outputs of whitened isotropic noise. Once interpolation has occurred, this model measures the inherent spectral geometry of <math id="A6.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> through the trace and log-determinant, and so it is directly measuring the implicit bias inherent in the learned weights. Examining the spectrum of weights to measure implicit model bias is a core aspect of HT-SR that motivated HTMP. Even though this auxiliary energy is not the Bayes free energy for the original dataset and prior-likelihood pair, we see in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> that for the third-layer convolutional weight of a ResNet50 trained on CIFAR-10, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> correlates surprisingly well with test accuracy during training, <span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">once training loss has plateaued</span>.
We see similar results for ResNet18 and ResNet34 on CIFAR-10 in <a href="#A8.F7" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. In <a href="#A8.F11" title="In H.4 Correlation of free energy with model quality across depth ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, we plot the correlation of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> with model quality across all layers, for ResNet50 on CIFAR-100 and all Pythia models. Interestingly, we see that every deeper layer for ResNet50 correlates very well with model quality (<math id="A6.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho&gt;0.9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho&gt;0.9}</annotation></semantics></math>). For the Pythia models, the Dense weight matrices seem to correlate very well across all layers and model sizes; however, for QueryKey weight matrices, the results are more mixed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Choice of precision parameter <math id="A6.SS3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To select <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> when comparing model quality with <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> across epochs of training <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we take two general approaches:</p>
<ol id="A6.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.3em;">
<li id="A6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A6.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1.</span></span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As detailed in <a href="#Thmremark1" title="Remark 1. ‣ 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Remark</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we set <math id="A6.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> at each epoch <math id="A6.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A6.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2.</span></span> 
<div id="A6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A6.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the epoch when test error is minimized. Then, we set <math id="A6.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id="A6.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> remains constant.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We find in our experiments that the second option works best for CV models. In fact, taking the first option for <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> results in a very poor correlation for the CV models. In comparison, both options work for the LLM models. To see why, we note the following. By <a href="#Thmlemma7" title="Lemma 7 (First and Second Moment). ‣ D.2 First and second moments ‣ Appendix D Derivation of limiting free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{1}=h/2\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{1}=h/2\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=2\gamma\mu_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=2\gamma\mu_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. As <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}=2\gamma/\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}=2\gamma/\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, then if we set <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1/\mu_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1/\mu_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. Hence, by selecting <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we are explicitly assuming that <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is already at its optimal value <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. As seen in <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#A8.F8" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> moving through <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> directly correlates with under- and over-fitting in CV models; taking <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> destroys this behavior. In comparison, we see in <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Using HTMP to understand training dynamics ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#A8.F9" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> that for the LLM models, <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}\approx h^{*}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}\approx h^{*}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> at each epoch. Hence, taking <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> does not alter the correlation. Similar behaviour has arisen in the literature: in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>, the spectral size <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> correlated strongly with model quality for well-trained networks within a model class, alongside metrics such as the tail exponent <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>. In comparison, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2023)</a></cite> demonstrated that for LLMs, <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> was <span id="A6.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">anti-correlated</span> with model quality, suggesting that spectral size plays a differing role for measuring model quality of LLMs versus CV models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Being able to correctly predict the optimal <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> value, i.e., <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{t}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, would enable our framework to accurately measure the amount of overfitting during training, and it is an important avenue for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Relation of optimal HTMP parameters to heavy-tailed results in literature</h3>

<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now detail similarities between the optimal scale-based heaviness derived in <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and those derived in the literature.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While previous work in the heavy-tailed literature consider mainly the tail behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bartlett et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agrawal et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, the fact that the first moment is proportional to <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> suggests that a distribution’s mean shares importance with tail behavior.
This also suggests deeper connections between heavy-tailed metrics and Geometric Complexity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dherin et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, discussed previously.
We see that the optimal heaviness <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}=2\gamma/\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}=2\gamma/\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> is a function of the aspect ratio <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>; dependence of heavy-tails on the aspect ratio was argued for in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
If we consider normalized heaviness <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{h}=\lambda\kappa/2\gamma\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{h}=\lambda\kappa/2\gamma\beta</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\mu_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\mu_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>), we find <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{h}^{*}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{h}^{*}=1</annotation></semantics></math>.
This is remarkably similar to the work of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bartlett et al. (2020)</a></cite>, where the minimum-norm solution for over-parameterized linear regression provides good generalization performance if power-law exponent on the linear feature covariance is equal to <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>.
A similar finding for DNNs was shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agrawal et al. (2022)</a></cite>.
Defining <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{h}=\lambda\kappa/\gamma\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{h}=\lambda\kappa/\gamma\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, optimal heaviness <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{h}^{*}=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{h}^{*}=2</annotation></semantics></math> places us in the moderately-heavy tailed universal class of HT-SR, which is expected to perform well <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin and Mahoney, 2021</a>)</cite>.
The clear numerical connection between these previous works and ours is surprising and motivating, despite our differing definitions and matrices.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Experimental details</h2>

<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>ResNets during training</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ResNet models used were each trained for <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>200</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200</annotation></semantics></math> epochs on the CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100 dataset. For the optimizer, stochastic gradient descent was used, with momentum <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, batch size <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math>, learning rate <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.02</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.02</annotation></semantics></math>, and weight-decay <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.0001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.0001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.0001</annotation></semantics></math>. No data-augmentation nor dropout was used, so as not to “over-regularize” the weight matrices, preventing clear heavy-tailed ESD shapes. We followed the experimental details of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hodgkinson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and we normalized the input data to have zero mean and unit variance per channel, as well as normalized each input vector <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf x}</annotation></semantics></math> to have norm <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||{\bf x}||=\sqrt{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mi>d</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||{\bf x}||=\sqrt{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=3\times 32\times 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=3\times 32\times 32</annotation></semantics></math>. We initialized the networks using the LeCun normal initialization. Each network was randomly initialized and trained <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> times. Checkpoints were taken every <math id="A7.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> epochs. These models were run on an H<math id="A7.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> GPU.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Fitting the HTMP</h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To fit the <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution to the ESD for <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\textnormal{spec}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau\text{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>spec</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>I</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\textnormal{spec}}({\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}-\tau\text{I})</annotation></semantics></math>, for trained weight matrix <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}\in\real^{d_{l-1}\times d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we firstly fix <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=d_{l}/d_{l-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=d_{l}/d_{l-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. For some weight matrices, we trim the top and bottom <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> eigenvalues, as these extreme eigenvalues can make fitting more difficult.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math> be the eigenvalues of <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{W}}_{l}^{T}{\mathbf{W}}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. Using the HTMP CDF from <a href="#Thmlemma4" title="Lemma 4 (CDF HTMP). ‣ C.1 Derivation of CDF for HTMP ‣ Appendix C High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur distribution ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, denoted <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>, we minimize the two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance,</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To compute <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}(\omega_{i}-\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}(\omega_{i}-\tau)</annotation></semantics></math>, then if <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2</annotation></semantics></math> is <span id="A7.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">not</span> an integer, then we can take <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ω</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and compute the principal argument</p>
<table id="A7.EGx78" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A7.Ex96"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A7.Ex96.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\theta_{i}=\text{atan2}\left(\mathcal{I}(a,b,\beta(\omega_{i}-\tau)),\mathcal{R}(a,b,\beta(\omega_{i}-\tau))\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>atan2</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\theta_{i}=\text{atan2}\left(\mathcal{I}(a,b,\beta(\omega_{i}-\tau)),\mathcal{R}(a,b,\beta(\omega_{i}-\tau))\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A7.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=\kappa/2,b=1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=\kappa/2,b=1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> are the imaginary and real parts of <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{y\downarrow 0}U(a,b,-x-iy)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{y\downarrow 0}U(a,b,-x-iy)</annotation></semantics></math>, given in <a href="#Thmlemma5" title="Lemma 5 (Non-Integer Evaluation of HTMP CDF). ‣ C.1 Derivation of CDF for HTMP ‣ Appendix C High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur distribution ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Then, as <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\theta_{i}\in(-\pi,\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{i}\in(-\pi,\pi]</annotation></semantics></math>, we can use an unwrapping operation (implemented numerically in common computing packages), that takes a set <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{d_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{d_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and adds integer multiples of <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> to the values in this set whenever the principal argument has passed through the boundary cut. This will return a set <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{1},\dots,\Theta_{d_{l}}\in[0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{1},\dots,\Theta_{d_{l}}\in[0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>, such that <math id="A7.SS2.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}(\omega_{i}-\tau)=2\Theta_{i}/\pi\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta}(\omega_{i}-\tau)=2\Theta_{i}/\pi\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the case when <math id="A7.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="A7.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">is</span> an integer, one must instead compute <math id="A7.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{y\downarrow 0}U\left(\kappa/2,1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2;-\beta x-i\beta y\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{y\downarrow 0}U\left(\kappa/2,1-\kappa/2\gamma+\kappa/2;-\beta x-i\beta y\right)</annotation></semantics></math> using complex numerical functions (such as the implementation of <math id="A7.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U(a,b,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U(a,b,z)</annotation></semantics></math> in the <span id="A7.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mpmath</span> package), in order to compute the CDF. This process is numerically much slower.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Further experimental results</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we will give further experimental details, that did not fit in the main body.</p>
</div>
<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Permuted label experiment</h3>

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now demonstrate that even on a task where no feature learning can occur, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> closely follows model quality; further, the HTMP analysis of <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> can still predict the optimal model over training. For this task, we train ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 where all training labels have been randomly permuted. Hence, training inputs <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf x}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf x}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are now independent of training outputs <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf y}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf y}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. For this task, the Bayes optimal accuracy is <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., random guessing for <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10</annotation></semantics></math> classes. Instead of accuracy, the appropriate metric to consider is cross-entropy on the test dataset. An optimal model will produce a prediction of <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{softmax}({\bf f}({\bf x}_{i}^{*};{\mathbf{W}},\phi))=[0.1]^{10}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mn>10</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{softmax}({\bf f}({\bf x}_{i}^{*};{\mathbf{W}},\phi))=[0.1]^{10}</annotation></semantics></math> for each input <math id="A8.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf x}_{i}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf x}_{i}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> in a test dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#A8.F6" title="In H.1 Permuted label experiment ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (top left) we see that HTMP still provides an excellent fit to the weight matrices in this case. Here, the weight matrix used for analysis is the third-layer convolutional weight matrix. We plot test error, empirical and asymptotic free energy against training epochs in <a href="#A8.F6" title="In H.1 Permuted label experiment ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (top right), for <math id="A8.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=4.72" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>4.72</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=4.72</annotation></semantics></math>, where we see a very strong correlation (<math id="A8.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\rho=0.819}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold">0.819</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\rho=0.819}</annotation></semantics></math>). We mark with a dotted line the epoch when training accuracy reaches <math id="A8.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99\%</annotation></semantics></math>, which we loosely interpret as <span id="A8.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">interpolation</span>. While the absolute scale of free energy does not differentiate between the untrained and trained models, once we constrain to interpolating epochs, the free energy very closely predicts test error.</p>
</div>
<div id="A8.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, we also see in <a href="#A8.F6" title="In H.1 Permuted label experiment ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> (bottom left) that after interpolating on the permuted training set, the optimal model corresponds to the one whose HTMP ratio <math id="A8.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is closest to <math id="A8.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> (in <a href="#A8.F6" title="In H.1 Permuted label experiment ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>(bottom right) we see that the assumptions of <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> are valid). Thus, even in this artificial learning task, our framework allows us to find what spectral properties the model is trying to optimize.</p>
</div>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A8.F6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">For ResNet18, trained on permuted CIFAR-10 dataset, we have the (top left) ESD (gray) and fitted <math id="A8.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\kappa,\gamma,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> distribution (red dotted lines), (top right) test CE, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-

                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and <math id="A8.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math>, vs. <math id="A8.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math> for <span id="A8.F6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">interpolating</span> epochs, and (bottom right) fitted HTMP parameters. Even for a task where there is no feature learning, our framework holds surprisingly well. Here, the weight matrix used for analysis is the third-layer convolutional weight.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.2 </span>Extra ResNet and Pythia models</h3>

<div id="A8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we provide further experimental evidence for the applicability of <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1. ‣ 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for analyzing training dynamics of large DNNs. Specifically, we repeat the analysis for ResNet18 and ResNet34 trained on CIFAR-10, and for the Pythia <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.8</annotation></semantics></math>B and Pythia <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.9</annotation></semantics></math>B models. We see in <a href="#A8.F7" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#A8.F8" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and <a href="#A8.F9" title="In H.2 Extra ResNet and Pythia models ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> that for CV models, overfitting is a function of <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> moving through <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas for the LLM models, <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\approx h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>≈</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\approx h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> during training, and so <math id="A8.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> increasing results in an improved model fit.</p>
</div>

                                W
                              
                            </span></a>. <figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A8.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Test error, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and <math id="A8.F8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mi>λ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\infty}^{\lambda}</annotation></semantics></math> vs. fitted <math id="A8.F8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa/\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa/\beta</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A8.F8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>. For CV, <math id="A8.F8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> (purple cross) aligns with minimum error. For LLMs, <math id="A8.F8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is attained early, and increasing <math id="A8.F8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> lowers test error. Extra experimental results to accompany <a href="#S4.F4" title="In 4.2 Limiting free energy ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A8.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia_2.8b_6.9b_resnet18_resnet34_c10_htmp_parameters.svg" id="A8.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/130;" width="476" height="130"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A8.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fitted <math id="A8.F9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">HTMP</mtext><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>κ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textbf{HTMP}_{\gamma,\kappa,\beta,\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters at each epoch. Extra experimental results to accompany <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Using HTMP to understand training dynamics ‣ 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.3 </span>ESDs</h3>

<div id="A8.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we provide ESDs for ResNet50 trained on CIFAR-10 and Pythia-<math id="A8.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1B</annotation></semantics></math> trained on Pile, to accompany the results given in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Note that the ESD for the other two models in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> were given in <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
