</figure>
</section>
<section id="A8.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.4 </span>Correlation of free energy with model quality across depth</h3>

<div id="A8.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Though we derived <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for the final-layer weights, a natural question is whether the correlation between free energy and model quality also holds for weights from deeper layers. We have already seen evidence of this in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4 Heavy-tails and free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for ResNet50 on CIFAR-10, where the free energy evaluated on the third-layer convolutional weight matrix correlated very strongly with model quality. We also provide theoretical motivation in <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Motivation for application of BFE-W for deeper layer weights ‣ Appendix F Further details ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>. Here, we provide extensive evaluation of correlation of free energy with model quality for deeper weights, across all weights of ResNet50 on CIFAR-100, and for Dense and QueryKey matrices at every layer for all Pythia models. We measure correlation from epoch <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> and epoch <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>43000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43000</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, so that training loss effects can be removed (remember <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> is derived for interpolating models). We provide the results in <a href="#A8.F11" title="In H.4 Correlation of free energy with model quality across depth ‣ Appendix H Further experimental results ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>. Interestingly, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for <span id="A8.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">every</span> weight for ResNet50 on CIFAR-100 correlates very strongly with model quality. We also see that <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is approximately constant across layers, and that distinct patterns emerge based on convolutional ordering (i.e., Conv 1 vs. Conv 2 weights seem to roughly double <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, and similarly for Conv 2. vs Conv. 3). For the Pythia models, the results are not as clear. For some models (e.g., Pythia <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.8</annotation></semantics></math>B), both QueryKey and Dense weight matrices at every layer show excellent correlation between <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and model quality; in contrast Pythia-<math id="A8.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="12" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>12</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12</annotation></semantics></math>B QueryKey weights show a very strong <span id="A8.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">anti-correlation</span> with model quality across most layers. This figure demonstrates that many weights can be used to evaluate <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>, though some care needs to be taken. Further, the relationship of <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> across layers and convolutional weights suggests that one may be able to derive the value of <math id="A8.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> based off of model parameters; this would allow for a priori prediction of when overfitting would occur.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="A8.F11.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/depth_corr_lam_resnet50_cifar100_lam_inv.svg" id="A8.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/173;" width="476" height="173"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="A8.F11.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.13123v1/pythia_depth_correlation.svg" id="A8.F11.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/173;" width="476" height="173"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F11.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A8.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Correlation of <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> with model quality for deeper weights, across (top) all weights of ResNet50 on CIFAR-100, and (bottom) for Dense and QueryKey matrices at every layer for all Pythia models. For the Pythia models, model quality is measured by log perplexity for the LAMBADA test dataset. We also provide the <math id="A8.F11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda^{*}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda^{*}=d_{l}/||{\mathbf{W}}_{l,t^{*}}||_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> value for all ResNet50 weights. We see that a significant proportion of deeper weights show a very strong correlation with model quality.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>Further empirical results for free energy</h2>

<section id="A9.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.1 </span>Comparison to HT-SR metrics</h3>

<div id="A9.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now directly compare <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> to the HT-SR metrics of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>, as defined in <a href="#S2" title="2 Related work &amp; background ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In this work, the metrics were computed using the WeightWatchers (WW) package <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin, 2024</a>)</cite>. To ensure fair comparison, we use the legacy version of WW (version <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.2.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2.7</annotation></semantics></math>) which is used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>. We compare <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> (primal) against <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{\infty}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{\infty}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|{\mathbf{W}}\|_{2\alpha}^{2\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (PL exponent), and <math id="A9.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> (ET-PL truncation).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="A9.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Spearman <math id="A9.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> correlation of model quality metrics with top-5 ImageNet test accuracy for <span id="A9.T1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Legacy</span> models. <figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="A9.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Spearman <math id="A9.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> correlation of model quality metrics with top-5 ImageNet test accuracy for <span id="A9.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CV</span> (non-dropout) models. Combined pools all models in this type. The <math id="A9.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are the fitted PL and ET-PL parameters. </span></figcaption>

</span></th>

<div id="A9.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Firstly, in <a href="#A9.T1" title="In I.1 Comparison to HT-SR metrics ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we compare <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> against the HT-SR metrics for the DNNs featured in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>, i.e., ResNet, VGG and DenseNet. We compare using the legacy model weight checkpoints used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martin et al. (2021)</a></cite>. The reported correlations are Spearmans <math id="A9.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> correlation. We see that, as expected, both within-group correlation and across-group correlation is approximately similar (and very strong) across <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and the HT-SR metrics, with the exception of VGG; as stated in <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Empirical evaluation ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, VGG employs <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">dropout</span> before the final-layer weights, and hence <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> performs very poorly on these models. Due to this, <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> has the <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">opposite</span> correlation with model quality across these groups. Further, we see that <math id="A9.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are poor predictors of model quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We now compare <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for all <span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">torchvision</span> models that are not <span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">dropout</span> or <span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">vision transformer</span> models. We use the most updated model weights as provided by <span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">torchvision</span>, as of May 2026. The results are displayed in <a href="#A9.T2" title="In I.1 Comparison to HT-SR metrics ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Here, while <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> correlates very strongly, we see that the HT-SR metrics now do not predict model quality across model classes. There is still some correlation within-group, i.e., for ResNeXt and Wide ResNet, though we observe that <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> is the most consistent predictor. Of particular note is that these metrics no longer predict test accuracy for ResNets. As the current available weights have been finely optimized for performance, it is perhaps the case that the weights have become over-regularized in some sense, and so one must develop further metrics (e.g., <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>) to evaluate test performance. We again see that <math id="A9.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are poor predictors of model quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.2 </span>When last-layer free energy does not predict model quality</h3>

<div id="A9.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As detailed in <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Empirical evaluation ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, certain classes of models do not show strong correlation between <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> and model quality for CV.</p>
<dl id="A9.I1" class="ltx_description">
<dt id="A9.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A9.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dropout.</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="A9.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Models that use dropout directly before the final-layer weights, such as VGG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015</a>)</cite>, EfficientNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan and Le, 2021</a>)</cite>, and MNASNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, do not show good correlation. This could be because the addition of dropout violates the <span id="A9.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">features</span> and <span id="A9.I1.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weights</span> decomposition of a neural network, or perhaps because dropout prevents complex correlations in the final-layer weights from occurring.</p>
</div></dd>
<dt id="A9.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A9.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision Transformers.</span></span></dt>
<dd class="ltx_item">
<div id="A9.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision transformers, e.g., ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dosovitskiy et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and Swin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, also do not show good correlation. We conjecture that a clear decomposition of vision transformers into <span id="A9.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">features</span> (final activations) and <span id="A9.I1.ix2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weight</span> (final layer) does not hold (though it does for language transformers).</p>
</div></dd>
</dl>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="A9.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Spearman <math id="A9.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> correlation of model quality metrics with top-5 ImageNet test accuracy for <span id="A9.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dropout</span> models. Combined pools all models in this type. The <math id="A9.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are the fitted PL and ET-PL parameters. </span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A9.T4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Spearman <math id="A9.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> correlation of model quality metrics with top-5 ImageNet test accuracy for <span id="A9.T4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision Transformer</span> models. Combined pools all models in this type. The <math id="A9.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are the fitted PL and ET-PL parameters. </span></figcaption>

<span id="A9.T4.6.4.8.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><math id="A9.T4.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.09" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.09</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.09</annotation></semantics></math></span>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="A9.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We provide the correlations for <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a>, as well as the HT-SR metrics, in <a href="#A9.T3" title="In I.2 When last-layer free energy does not predict model quality ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#A9.T4" title="In I.2 When last-layer free energy does not predict model quality ‣ Appendix I Further empirical results for free energy ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
For <span id="A9.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision Transformers</span>, the HT-SR metrics are also poor predictors of model quality. However, though correlation is only mild (<math id="A9.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.42\geq\rho\geq-0.66" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.42</mn></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.66</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.42\geq\rho\geq-0.66</annotation></semantics></math>), the HT-SR metrics are much stronger predictors than <a href="#S3.Ex4" title="In 3.2 Evaluation of free energy using final-layer weights ‣ 3 Free energy for trained weights ‣ Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">BFE-
                              
                                W
                              
                            </span></a> for the Dropout models. Interestingly, <math id="A9.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A9.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> still do not show consistent correlation.</p>
</div>
